what: Database concurrency control coordinates overlapping transactions so their committed effects meet the isolation guarantee. Techniques include locks, MVCC snapshots, optimistic validation, conflict detection, and serializable scheduling.
why: Concurrent execution improves utilization, but careless interleavings can lose updates, read inconsistent combinations, or violate cross-row invariants. The model must protect business rules, not just individual rows.
mental: Write each transaction as a sequence of reads and writes, then ask whether an interleaving could produce a result that no valid serial order would produce. The concurrency-control mechanism determines which schedules can commit.
points: Conflict serializability considers pairs of conflicting operations on the same data item where at least one is a write.
A precedence graph with a cycle indicates that a schedule is not conflict-serializable under the classic test.
Snapshot isolation can still allow anomalies such as write skew when transactions update disjoint rows based on overlapping reads.
Locks and serializable validation can block or abort conflicting transactions.
Application-level invariants spanning several rows may need explicit constraints, locking, or serializable transactions.
steps: Transaction A checks that fewer than ten reservations exist.
Transaction B checks the same condition before A commits.
Both insert different rows, so a simple row-level conflict may not expose the shared-count invariant.
Use a database constraint, a locking/serialization strategy, or a different schema that makes the invariant enforceable.
usage: Preventing lost updates and write skew.
Solving conflict-serializability graph questions.
Designing safe booking, inventory, and quota workflows.
mistakes: Assuming two transactions are safe because they update different rows.
Confusing a serial execution with any arbitrary interleaving.
Treating isolation-level labels as a substitute for reasoning about the actual invariant.

interview.q: What does conflict serializability mean?
interview.a: A schedule is conflict-serializable when its conflicting operation order is equivalent to some serial transaction order.

interview.q: How can write skew occur under snapshot isolation?
interview.a: Two transactions read a shared invariant from the same snapshot and update disjoint rows, allowing both to commit a combined state that violates the invariant.

title: Buffer Pool
summary: The database's cache of disk pages. Replacement policy, dirty pages, and checkpoints.
what: A buffer pool is the database-managed memory cache for database pages read from persistent storage. It tracks page frames, dirty state, pin/reference information, replacement candidates, and coordination so many query operators can reuse pages safely.
why: Disk access is much slower than memory access. A buffer pool reduces physical reads, amortizes repeated work, and mediates the timing of page writes, but an undersized or polluted pool can cause churn.
mental: Treat the buffer pool as a bounded cache of fixed-size pages. A query pins pages it needs while using them; replacement can reuse unpinned frames, and dirty pages need proper writeback before their frames are reused.
points: A page hit avoids a physical read when the page is already resident.
Dirty pages contain changes not yet written to the main data file.
Replacement policy selects eligible victim pages based on recency, frequency, or other workload signals.
WAL or another recovery method constrains when dirty pages may safely reach storage.
Pinning, latching, and transaction locks solve distinct problems: frame lifetime, in-memory consistency, and logical concurrency.
steps: A query requests a database page.
The buffer manager finds it in memory or reads it into a free/victim frame.
The query pins the page and synchronizes access while inspecting data.
Dirty pages are written back according to recovery and checkpoint rules; unpinned frames can then be reused.
usage: Explaining why repeated queries can be faster after warm-up.
Diagnosing buffer cache hit rate, dirty-page pressure, and read amplification.
Understanding the interaction between checkpoints, WAL, and storage.
mistakes: Assuming a high cache hit rate alone proves queries are efficient.
Evicting a page that is still pinned by an active operation.
Confusing an in-memory page latch with a transaction-level row lock.

interview.q: What is the difference between a buffer-pool hit and a cache hit at the application level?
interview.a: A buffer-pool hit means the database page is resident in the DBMS cache; application caches may avoid the database query entirely.

interview.q: Why can dirty pages not simply be discarded?
interview.a: Their changes may be the only current copy of committed or uncommitted page state; the recovery and writeback protocol must preserve correctness before reuse.
